title: The Messenger's Road — Mecca to Medina
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Guarded Sanctuary — the Year of the Elephant and the orphan of the Quraysh

stops.name: Mecca — the Sacred Mosque, the plain before the Kaaba
stops.campa: Abraha of the Yemen marches north with a great elephant to pull down God's House and turn the pilgrimage to his church at Sana'a. Abd al-Muttalib, keeper of the Kaaba, asks only for his stolen camels and leaves the House to its Owner. At the edge of the sacred valley the elephant kneels and will not advance on Mecca. Then from the sea flocks of ababil come, each bird bearing stones of baked clay, and they hurl them down upon the host until the army is left like eaten stalks, devoured. The House stands. This is the year the Messenger is born.
stops.quote: Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten straw.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and Masjid al-Haram, Mecca
Ottoman tile panels of the Sacred Mosque
Surah Al-Fil in early Hijazi Quran manuscript
sources: Ibn Ishaq / Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah

stops.name: Mecca — the house of the Banu Hashim, birthplace of the Prophet
stops.campa: In the month of Rabi al-Awwal, in the quarter of the Banu Hashim, Amina bint Wahb is delivered of a son. His father Abdullah is already dead, buried at Yathrib on the trade road; the child is an orphan from the first breath. Abd al-Muttalib carries the boy into the Kaaba and gives thanks, and names him Muhammad, the Praised, a name strange to the Arabs. Amina will say a light went out of her that lit the castles of Syria. The desert stars stand over Mecca, and the House keeps its newest son.
suggested_refs: Mawlid an-Nabi site, the traditional birthplace near Marwah, Mecca
Ottoman Mawlid manuscripts (hilye script, no figure)

stops.name: The country of the Banu Sa'd — the tents of Halima the wet-nurse
stops.campa: Halima of the Banu Sa'd comes to Mecca in a lean year seeking a nursling and finds only the orphan, whom the wealthier women pass over. She takes him for want of better, and at once her dry breast fills, her worn she-camel grows sleek, her flock returns fat while her neighbours' starve. Blessing follows the child into the desert. For years the Arab air and the pure tongue of the badiya are his schooling, until Halima marvels and, half-afraid of the wonders about him, brings him home to Amina.
suggested_refs: Bani Sa'd region, Taif highlands
Ottoman Siyer-i Nebi manuscript (text pages, Halima episode)

stops.name: The desert of the Banu Sa'd — the Opening of the Breast
stops.campa: As the boy plays among the lambs behind the tents, two men in white robes come to him and lay him down. They open his breast, draw forth his heart, and take from it a black clot, saying, this was the portion of Satan in you. They wash the heart in a golden basin with the water of Zamzam and set it back, and seal the breast. His foster-brother runs crying that the Qurayshi child is slain, but he is found standing, pale, unharmed, a mark upon his chest. Anas will say the trace of that stitching stayed on the Messenger's breast.
stops.quote: Then he took his heart out and extracted from it a blood-clot and said: This was the part of Satan in you. Then he washed it with the water of Zamzam in a golden basin and sealed it up and restored it to its place.
stops.quote_source: Sahih Muslim 162 (the splitting of the breast)
suggested_refs: Siyer-i Nebi text pages on the sharh al-sadr
the tradition of the Zamzam well, Masjid al-Haram

stops.name: Mecca — the well of Zamzam, the standing of Abd al-Muttalib
stops.campa: The grandfather who keeps the child is the same Abd al-Muttalib to whom, years before, God showed in a dream over three nights the buried well of Zamzam — the spring that gushed for Hagar and the infant Ishmael, lost and choked with sand since the days of Jurhum. He dug where the dream commanded and struck the water, and found the golden gazelles and the swords the old tribe had hidden there. Now, keeper of Zamzam and of the House, he seats the fatherless boy upon his own carpet beside the Kaaba, where his own sons may not sit, sensing a greatness upon him.
suggested_refs: The Well of Zamzam, Masjid al-Haram
the Zamzam gallery beneath the mataf

stops.name: Mecca — the guardianship of Abu Talib after Abd al-Muttalib
stops.campa: Amina dies at al-Abwa on the road from Yathrib, and the boy is doubly orphaned. Abd al-Muttalib takes him under his own cloak at the Kaaba, letting no one turn the child from his couch; but the old chief soon dies too. Guardianship passes to Abu Talib, poor but noble, who loves his brother's son above his own children, keeps him near, feeds him first. In this uncle's house the fatherless boy grows toward manhood, sheltered by a man who will defend him to the end and yet never speak the creed.
suggested_refs: al-Abwa, grave of Amina, on the Mecca–Medina road
Jannat al-Mu'alla cemetery, Mecca (Abd al-Muttalib)

stops.name: Bosra — the cell of the monk Bahira
stops.campa: Abu Talib takes the boy of some twelve years on the Syria caravan. At Bosra the monk Bahira, who reads the old books in his cell, sees a low cloud shading one rider alone and the branches of a tree bending over him where he sits. He calls the whole caravan to a meal, watches the boy, and finding at last the seal of prophethood between his shoulders as the scriptures foretold, warns Abu Talib: guard your nephew from the Jews and the Romans, for a great destiny is upon him. Return him home. Send him back to Mecca.
stops.quote: Take your nephew back to his country and guard him carefully against the Jews, for by God, if they see him and know about him what I know, they will do him evil.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Bahira episode)
suggested_refs: Ruins of the Monastery of Bahira (Dayr Bahira), Bosra, Syria
Roman theatre and old town of Bosra

segments.name: Al-Amin — the trusted youth, Khadija, and the Black Stone

stops.name: Mecca — the markets and the byname al-Amin
stops.campa: The youth grows in Mecca honest above his fellows, keeping his word, shunning the idols and the drinking of his age. The Quraysh, who quarrel and cheat in trade, come to trust him so wholly that they call him al-Amin, the Trustworthy, and leave their goods in his keeping. He tends flocks on the hills as the prophets did before him, and joins the pact of the Fudul sworn to defend the wronged in Mecca. Among a people of many gods he keeps, without a book, a straight and quiet way.
suggested_refs: Mount Abu Qubays overlooking the Kaaba
the wells and markets of old Mecca

stops.name: Mecca — the house of Khadija bint Khuwaylid, the marriage
stops.campa: Khadija, a noble widow and merchant, hires the trusted youth to lead her caravan to Syria. Her servant Maysara returns full of his honesty and of wonders on the road — two angels shading him from the sun. Khadija, twice widowed and forty, sends to offer herself in marriage; he is about twenty-five. They wed, and she bears him his children and stands as the rock of his life. First of all creatures she will believe him; her wealth and her love shelter the years before the light comes down.
suggested_refs: Site of the house of Khadija, Mecca (excavated foundations)
Ottoman calligraphic panels naming Khadija among the Mothers of the Believers

stops.name: Mecca — the rebuilding of the Kaaba and the raising of the Black Stone
stops.campa: A flood and fire have damaged the Kaaba, and the clans rebuild it; but when the Black Stone must be lifted to its corner every clan claims the honour and swords are half-drawn. They agree the next man through the gate shall judge. It is al-Amin. This is the Trustworthy — we accept him, they cry. He spreads his cloak upon the ground, lays the Stone upon it, and bids the elders of every clan take hold of the edges and raise it together; then with his own hand he sets it in its place. So he keeps the peace of the House.
suggested_refs: The Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad) in its silver casing, Kaaba
the eastern corner (Rukn al-Aswad) of the Kaaba

stops.name: Jabal al-Nur — the retreats to the Cave of Hira
stops.campa: As the fortieth year nears, a love of solitude comes upon him. He climbs the sharp black peak of Jabal al-Nur, the Mountain of Light, above Mecca and shuts himself in the narrow cave of Hira for nights together, taking provision, worshipping the one God of Abraham after the manner of the hanifs, and returning to Khadija for more. True visions begin to come to him like the breaking of dawn. The valley of Mecca and its House lie small below; the cave waits for the Word.
suggested_refs: Cave of Hira (Ghar Hira) on Jabal al-Nur, near Mecca
the ascent of Jabal al-Nur

segments.name: Iqra — the descent of the Revelation and the first believers

stops.name: Cave of Hira — the Night of Power, Gabriel and the command to Read
stops.campa: On a night of Ramadan the angel Gabriel comes to him in the cave and commands: Read! He answers, I am not one who reads. The angel seizes and presses him until he can bear no more, releases him, and says again, Read; three times, until the strength is gone from him. Then come the first words ever sent down: Read in the name of thy Lord who created, created man from a clinging clot. Read, and thy Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen. The Word of God has entered the world.
stops.quote: Read in the name of your Lord who created — created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man that which he knew not.
suggested_refs: Cave of Hira, Jabal al-Nur
Surah Al-Alaq in a Kufic Quran folio

stops.name: Mecca — the flight home, the cloak of Khadija, the words of Waraqa
stops.campa: He comes down the mountain trembling, his heart beating hard, and reaches Khadija crying, Cover me, cover me! She wraps him until the fear leaves, then says: God will never disgrace you; you keep good relations, bear the burdens of others, speak the truth. She takes him to her cousin Waraqa, an old blind Christian who knows the scriptures, and Waraqa declares: This is the Namus that came to Moses. Would that I were young when your people drive you out. Driven out? he asks. Yes, Waraqa says — no man brought the like without being fought.
stops.quote: This is the Namus (Gabriel) whom Allah sent to Moses. I wish I were young and could live up to the time when your people would turn you out. Would they drive me out? Yes, never came a man with the like of what you have brought but was treated with hostility.
suggested_refs: Site of the house of Khadija, Mecca
early Hijazi Quran manuscript (Birmingham folios)

stops.name: Mecca — the first believers: Khadija, Ali, Abu Bakr, Zayd
stops.campa: The Word continues to descend, and the first hands are stretched out to it. Khadija believes before any other, the first of all the ummah. Ali, the boy of the house whom the Prophet raised, believes though still a child; Zayd, the freed servant and adopted son, believes; and among the men Abu Bakr, whose word carries weight in Mecca, believes at once and brings others after him. They pray in secret in the ravines and houses of Mecca, a hidden congregation, while the idols still stand in the House.
suggested_refs: Dar al-Arqam site, Mecca (the early meeting house)
calligraphic roundels of the first companions, Ottoman mosques

stops.name: Mecca — the open call and the persecution of the Quraysh
stops.campa: Commanded to proclaim openly, he climbs Mount Safa and warns his clans of the Reckoning, and calls them from many gods to the One. The Quraysh, fearing for the House and their trade, turn on him. They mock, they throw filth as he prays, they set the entrails of a slaughtered camel on his back at the Kaaba; his daughter comes weeping to clean him. The weak among the believers are seized and beaten. Yet the recitation keeps descending, and the little band holds, praying toward the House.
stops.quote: Proclaim what you are commanded, and turn away from the polytheists. Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers.
suggested_refs: Mount Safa, Masjid al-Haram
Quran 15 (Al-Hijr) in an early manuscript

stops.name: Mecca — Bilal on the burning sands, 'One! One!'
stops.campa: Bilal the Abyssinian, slave of Umayya ibn Khalaf, will not renounce the One God. His master drags him out into the noon of Mecca, throws him on the scorching sand, and lays a great rock upon his chest to crush the faith from him. Through the heat Bilal answers only, Ahad, Ahad — One, One. Abu Bakr passes, sees the torment, and buys him free. So the tortured slave becomes a freedman of the faith, and one day his voice, first of all voices, will call the prayer from the roof of the Kaaba.
stops.quote: Ahad! Ahad!  (One! One!)
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the trial of Bilal)
suggested_refs: the plain of al-Batha, Mecca
later shrine tradition of Bilal at Damascus

stops.name: Aksum — the emigration to Abyssinia and the court of the Negus
stops.campa: As the persecution hardens, the Messenger sends a band of the weak across the sea to the Christian king of Abyssinia, the Negus, a just ruler under whom none is wronged. When the Quraysh send envoys demanding the refugees back, the Negus summons them; Ja'far, cousin of the Prophet, speaks for the faith and recites the sura of Mary — the words on Jesus and his virgin mother. The king weeps into his beard and marks a line on the ground: what you have brought and what Jesus brought come from one lamp. He shelters them, and will not give them up.
stops.quote: This and what Jesus brought have come from the same niche of light. Go, for you are safe in my land; I will not give you up.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the first migration to Abyssinia)
suggested_refs: Kingdom of Aksum, Ethiopia (the Negus's court)
Al-Nejashi Mosque, Negash, Tigray — traditional burial of the Negus
Surah Maryam (19) in an early Quran folio

segments.name: The Year of Sorrow — the boycott, the deaths, Ta'if, and the Night Journey

stops.name: Mecca — the ravine of Abu Talib, the three-year boycott
stops.campa: The Quraysh hang a written pact in the Kaaba: none shall trade with, marry, or speak to the Banu Hashim until they surrender the Prophet. For nearly three years the clan is penned in the ravine of Abu Talib, hungry, the cries of the children heard beyond the rocks, sustained only by what friends can smuggle in. Then the Prophet tells his uncle that God has sent a creeping thing upon the document and eaten all but the name of God. They open the Kaaba; it is as he said, and the shamed chiefs tear the boycott down.
suggested_refs: Shi'b Abi Talib, the ravine below Jabal Abu Qubays, Mecca
the traditional cemetery of Jannat al-Mu'alla nearby

stops.name: Mecca — the Year of Sorrow, the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib
stops.campa: In one bitter year the two who sheltered him are taken. Khadija dies, the first believer, the wife of twenty-five years, in whose love he found rest and in whose arms he wept his first fear. And Abu Talib dies, the uncle who guarded him from the Quraysh though he never spoke the creed. Grief lies heavy on the Messenger; the year is named the Year of Sorrow. The protection about him is stripped away, and the Quraysh grow bolder against him now that the old lion is gone.
suggested_refs: Jannat al-Mu'alla cemetery, Mecca (graves of Khadija and Abu Talib)
Ottoman hilye naming Khadija

stops.name: Ta'if — the stoning and the supplication
stops.campa: Seeking new ground for the faith, he goes up to Ta'if in the cool hills with Zayd. The chiefs rebuff him and set the slaves and boys to line the road and pelt him with stones until his sandals fill with blood. Bruised, he shelters in a garden and lifts a supplication of pure surrender: to You I complain of my weakness; if You are not angry with me I do not care. Gabriel comes with the angel of the mountains, offering to crush the two hills of Mecca upon them. He refuses: rather, that God bring from their loins a people who worship Him alone.
stops.quote: O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my scarcity of resources, and my lowliness before men. You are the Lord of the weak, and You are my Lord. If You are not angry with me I do not care, but Your protection is more expansive for me.
stops.quote_source: The Supplication of Ta'if (Ibn Ishaq; al-Tabarani)
suggested_refs: Mosque of Addas / the garden tradition, Ta'if
the walls of old Ta'if

stops.name: Mecca — the Sacred Mosque, Buraq and the start of the Night Journey
stops.campa: As he lies near the Kaaba, in the place called al-Hijr, Gabriel comes and splits his breast once more, washing the heart with Zamzam and filling it with faith and wisdom. Then is brought Buraq, a white beast smaller than a mule and larger than an ass, whose stride reaches as far as its eye can see. Mounted upon it, with Gabriel beside him, the Messenger is carried in a single night out of the Sacred Mosque and northward over the sleeping earth, toward the Farthest Mosque at Jerusalem. Glory be to Him who took His servant by night.
stops.quote: Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs.
suggested_refs: the Hijr / Hatim of the Kaaba
Ottoman Miraj-nama illuminations (Buraq depicted without a human face for the Prophet)

stops.name: Jerusalem — the Farthest Mosque, the Prophet leads the prophets in prayer
stops.campa: Buraq alights at the Noble Sanctuary, at the Rock from which Solomon's Temple rose, and the Messenger tethers the beast at the ring where the prophets tied theirs. He enters the Farthest Mosque, and there the messengers of God are gathered — Abraham, Moses, Jesus and all the rest. Gabriel sets him forward, and Muhammad leads the whole assembly of prophets in prayer, imam of them all. Two vessels are offered him, wine and milk; he chooses the milk, and Gabriel says: you have chosen the right nature, the fitrah, for your people.
suggested_refs: The Noble Rock (as-Sakhrah) under the Dome of the Rock, Jerusalem
Al-Aqsa Mosque, al-Haram al-Sharif
the ring of Buraq at the western wall (tradition)

stops.name: The Seven Heavens — the ascent past the prophets (the Mi'raj)
stops.campa: From the Rock, upon a ladder of light, the ascent begins. At the first heaven's gate stands Adam, father of mankind, greeting his righteous son. In the heavens above dwell Jesus and John the Baptist together, then Joseph of surpassing beauty, then Idris raised to a high place, then Aaron, then Moses who weeps that this later prophet's people shall outnumber his own. Gabriel names each and each welcomes him: welcome, righteous prophet and righteous son. Higher still than any before him, the servant of God is carried up.
stops.quote: Then I was made to ascend to the second heaven... and there were Jesus, son of Mary, and John, son of Zechariah. Every time I passed a prophet he welcomed me and said: Welcome, O righteous prophet and righteous brother.
suggested_refs: Ottoman/Timurid Miraj-nama manuscript pages (the seven heavens)
the Dome of the Ascension (Qubbat al-Mi'raj), al-Haram al-Sharif

stops.name: The Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary — the fifty prayers brought down to five
stops.campa: At the seventh heaven Abraham leans against the Much-Frequented House, where seventy thousand angels enter each day and return no more. Beyond it stands the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, its leaves like the ears of elephants, veiled in colours no tongue can tell; here the ascent ends and the prayers are ordained — fifty each day. Passing Moses, he is sent back, and again, and again, to plead them lower, until they are five, yet counted as fifty in reward. I have asked my Lord until I am ashamed, he says, and accepts.
stops.quote: These are five prayers and they are all equal to fifty in reward, for My Word does not change. I felt ashamed to return to my Lord again.
suggested_refs: Sidrat al-Muntaha in Miraj-nama illumination
the Bayt al-Ma'mur tradition

segments.name: The Hijra — the plot, the Cave of Thawr, and the road to Yathrib

stops.name: Mecca — the pledges of Aqaba, the Yathrib men swear allegiance
stops.campa: At the hill of Aqaba, in the pilgrim season, men from Yathrib meet the Messenger by night and pledge themselves to him: to worship none but God, to obey, to protect him as they protect their own wives and children. This is the second pledge of Aqaba, some seventy-three men and two women, the seed of the Helpers. They ask for a teacher of the recitation and he sends one back with them. Islam has found a city that will open its gates. The way of the emigration is prepared.
suggested_refs: the hill of Aqaba near Mina
the Jamarat valley, Mina

stops.name: Mecca — the plot of the Quraysh and Ali in the bed
stops.campa: The chiefs of Quraysh gather in their council house and resolve to kill him, one young man from each clan to strike together so no single tribe can be blamed. That night they ring his house with swords. But the Messenger lays Ali in his bed under the green cloak, to give back the trusts left in his keeping, and walks out through the assassins, casting dust as he passes and reciting; and their eyes are held so they see him not. God has undone their plotting. He goes to Abu Bakr, and the two slip out of Mecca.
stops.quote: And remember when the disbelievers plotted against you to imprison you, or kill you, or drive you out. They plot, but Allah also plans. And Allah is the best of planners.
suggested_refs: the house of the Prophet, Mecca (traditional site)
Dar an-Nadwa (the council house) site near the Kaaba

stops.name: The Cave of Thawr — the spider's web, the dove, 'God is with us'
stops.campa: South of Mecca they climb Mount Thawr and hide in its cave three nights while the Quraysh hunt them, a reward on their heads. The trackers come to the very mouth of the cave; Abu Bakr trembles, for the pursuers are so near that if one looked at his feet he would see the two below. But a spider has spun her web across the opening and a dove has nested and laid, so the men judge no one has entered, and turn away. Do not grieve, the Prophet says; God is with us.
stops.quote: Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.  (When they were two in the cave, and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.)
suggested_refs: Cave of Thawr (Ghar Thawr) on Jabal Thawr, south of Mecca
the ascent of Jabal Thawr

stops.name: The desert road — the pursuit of Suraqa ibn Malik
stops.campa: They strike out for Yathrib along back-ways by the coast. Suraqa ibn Malik, lured by the Quraysh bounty, gives chase on his swift horse and nearly overtakes them; but three times the forelegs of his mount sink into the firm ground and cast him, until he understands he rides against a power he cannot beat. He begs quarter, and the Messenger, who promised him the bracelets of the Persian king, grants him a writ of safety. The hunter turns back to hide the trail he came by. The road north lies open.
suggested_refs: the old Mecca–Medina coastal caravan route
waymarks of the Hijra trail (modern Hijrah Trail markers)
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (the Hijra narration of Suraqa)

stops.name: Quba — the first mosque, arrival at the edge of Yathrib
stops.campa: At Quba, on the outskirts of Yathrib, the emigrant is received with joy; the people climb their roofs crying that the full moon has risen over them. Here he stays some days and lays with his own hands the foundation of the first mosque of Islam, a square of palm-trunks and mud, and prays in it — a house of God built for prayer upon piety from the first day. Ali, left to return the trusts, catches up with him. Then the Messenger mounts his she-camel to enter the city itself.
stops.quote: A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in; within it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.
suggested_refs: Quba Mosque (Masjid Quba), Medina — the first mosque
Quran 9:108 in an early manuscript

segments.name: The City of the Prophet — Medina, the mosque, and the covenant

stops.name: Medina — the camel Qaswa chooses the ground of the mosque
stops.campa: He rides into Yathrib and every clan seizes his camel's halter, each begging him to lodge with them. Leave her, he says; she is commanded of God. Qaswa walks on through the town and at last kneels of her own accord upon a drying-yard belonging to two orphan boys of the Banu Najjar. Here, God willing, is the place. He buys the plot, refusing it as a gift, and lodges meanwhile with Abu Ayyub. On this ground rises the Mosque of the Prophet, plain-built, his own home and the heart of the new community.
stops.quote: Leave her, for she is commanded (by God).
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the choosing of the mosque's site)
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
the site of the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari

stops.name: Medina — the Constitution and the brotherhood of Emigrants and Helpers
stops.campa: The town, once torn between Aws and Khazraj, is knit into one body. The Messenger writes a covenant binding Emigrants and Helpers, and the Jewish clans beside them, into a single community: one hand against any aggressor, blood and ransom shared, the disputes referred to God and His Messenger. And man by man he pairs each Meccan emigrant with a Medinan Helper as brothers in faith, so the poor and homeless are taken into houses and share in goods. From two cities and many tribes, one ummah is made.
stops.quote: They are one community distinct from other people. The believers shall not leave anyone destitute among them... Whenever you differ about a matter, it must be referred to God and to Muhammad.
stops.quote_source: The Constitution (Sahifa) of Medina, in Ibn Ishaq
suggested_refs: the Constitution of Medina text (Ibn Ishaq)
Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Medina
sources: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Sahifa)

stops.name: Medina — the change of the Qibla toward the Sacred Mosque
stops.campa: For months in Medina the believers pray toward Jerusalem, but the Prophet turns his face up to heaven longing for a sign. Then the command descends: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. In the midst of prayer, in the mosque that keeps the memory, the whole congregation wheels round from north to south, from the Farthest Mosque to the House of Abraham at Mecca. So the qibla of the new faith is fixed on the Kaaba, and the Muslims of all the earth thereafter face the ancient House when they stand before God.
stops.quote: We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qibla with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.
suggested_refs: Masjid al-Qiblatayn (the Mosque of the Two Qiblas), Medina
Quran 2:144 in an early Quran folio

segments.name: The Battles of the Faith — Badr, Uhud, the Trench, Hudaybiyya

stops.name: Badr — the wells, the angels at the ranks
stops.campa: At the wells of Badr the small band of believers, some three hundred, meets the army of Quraysh near a thousand strong. The Messenger stands in prayer through the night, and God sends down His help: a rain to firm the sand under the faithful, and angels in their thousands descending upon the ranks. In the morning the Quraysh are broken and their proud chiefs slain, Abu Jahl among them. It is the day God called the Day of Distinction, when truth was parted from falsehood, and the young community is saved.
stops.quote: Your Lord will reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down. Yes, if you remain patient and conscious of God, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels having marks of distinction.
suggested_refs: Battlefield and wells of Badr, Al Madinah Province
the martyrs' cemetery at Badr

stops.name: Mount Uhud — the wound and the broken tooth
stops.campa: The next spring the Quraysh come for revenge below Mount Uhud. The archers set on the hill leave their post when they see plunder, and the Muslims are caught from behind. The Messenger himself is struck; his face is cut, a tooth is broken, the rings of his helmet driven into his cheek. A cry runs that he is slain, and hearts fail — but he is living, and rallies the faithful to the mountain. His uncle Hamza, the Lion of God, lies dead among the martyrs. The victory of Badr is answered with a wound, and a hard lesson in obedience.
stops.quote: Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?
suggested_refs: Mount Uhud and the archers' hill (Jabal al-Rumat), Medina
the graves of the martyrs of Uhud, including Hamza

stops.name: Medina — the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq)
stops.campa: A great confederacy of Quraysh and their allies, ten thousand, marches to end Medina. On Salman's counsel the believers dig a trench across the open approaches to the city — a thing the Arabs have never seen — and the Prophet digs with them, hungry, binding a stone to his belly. As they strike the rock a spark leaps and he foretells the castles of Syria, Persia, Yemen laid open to the faith. For weeks the host is held at the ditch. Then God sends a bitter wind that overturns their tents and scatters them in the night, unfought.
stops.quote: O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see.
suggested_refs: the site of the trench near Jabal Sila', Medina (the Seven Mosques)
Quran 33 (Al-Ahzab) in manuscript

stops.name: Al-Hudaybiyya — the treaty and the pledge under the tree
stops.campa: Bound for the pilgrimage in white, unarmed, the Messenger is halted at Hudaybiyya on the edge of the sacred ground. His camel Qaswa kneels and will not go on: the same One who held the elephant holds her back. Under a tree the believers pledge to him unto death, the Pledge of Good Pleasure. A treaty is cut with the Quraysh — a ten-year truce, return this year, pilgrimage the next — that seems a defeat and is named by God a clear victory, for it opens the roads and the tongues, and men enter the faith in crowds.
stops.quote: Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory.
suggested_refs: Al-Hudaybiyya (al-Shumaysi), on the edge of the Meccan haram
the tree of the Ridwan pledge (traditional site)

stops.name: Medina — the letters to the kings of the earth
stops.campa: Peace won at Hudaybiyya, the Messenger turns to the wide world. He has a silver seal graven, Muhammad the Messenger of God, and sends emissaries with letters to the great rulers, calling them to the One God: to Heraclius the Roman, to Chosroes of Persia, to the Muqawqis of Egypt, to his old friend the Negus. Heraclius reads and honours the letter; Chosroes tears it and is warned his kingdom shall be torn likewise; the Negus believes. So from the small oasis-state the summons of Islam goes out to the thrones of the age.
stops.quote: In the name of God, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, servant of God and His Messenger, to Heraclius the great one of the Romans. Peace be upon him who follows the guidance. I call you with the call of Islam; accept Islam and you shall be safe.
stops.quote_source: The letter to Heraclius, in Sahih al-Bukhari 7 and Ibn Ishaq
suggested_refs: the seal of the Prophet (naqsh, Muhammad rasul Allah)
the traditional letter to Heraclius (relic manuscripts)

stops.name: Khaybar — the fall of the fortress oasis
stops.campa: Northward the Messenger leads his men against the fortified Jewish oasis of Khaybar, whose towers and date-groves have harboured his enemies. He gives the banner to Ali, saying it goes to one who loves God and His Messenger and whom they love; and Ali, his eye healed by the Prophet's spittle, takes the great fort of Qamus, striking down the champion Marhab. Khaybar falls, and its lands are left to their people as tenants, giving half their harvest. On the way home the true nature of the faith is tested and the community is enriched and secured.
stops.quote: Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves God and His Messenger, and God and His Messenger love him; God will grant victory through his hands.
suggested_refs: Khaybar fort (Qal'at al-Qamus) and oasis, Madinah Province
the old town and date palms of Khaybar

stops.name: Mu'ta — the martyrs beyond the Jordan
stops.campa: The faith reaches the borders of Rome. Three thousand are sent north to Mu'ta beyond the Jordan against a vast Byzantine and Arab host. Zayd, the beloved freedman, bears the banner and falls; Ja'far takes it and, his hands struck off, clasps it to his breast until he too is slain — God gives him wings in Paradise, and he is called Ja'far of the Two Wings. Abdullah ibn Rawaha falls after. Then Khalid ibn al-Walid takes up the standard and, by a cunning withdrawal, brings the small army home unbroken from an impossible field.
suggested_refs: the tombs of Ja'far, Zayd and Abdullah ibn Rawaha at Mazar, near al-Karak, Jordan
the site of the Battle of Mu'ta

segments.name: The Opening and the Return — Mecca conquered, the Farewell, the passing

stops.name: Mecca — the Conquest, the idols cast down from the Kaaba
stops.campa: The truce broken, the Messenger comes down upon Mecca with ten thousand, and the city that cast him out falls almost without a sword. He enters as conqueror, his head bowed low upon his camel in humility before God, and grants a general pardon: Go, you are free. Then he comes to the Kaaba where three hundred and sixty idols stand, and strikes them down one by one with his staff, reciting as they topple: Truth has come and falsehood has vanished. The ancient House of Abraham is cleansed at last and given back to the One God.
stops.quote: Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is bound to vanish.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba cleansed of idols, Masjid al-Haram
Quran 17:81 in calligraphy
the Maqam Ibrahim near the Kaaba

stops.name: Mecca — Bilal's call to prayer from atop the Kaaba
stops.campa: On the day of the Opening, the Messenger bids Bilal — once the slave crushed on the burning sand, crying One, One — climb upon the roof of the Kaaba itself and call the people to prayer. The freedman's voice rises over the conquered city: God is greatest; there is no god but God. Where the idols stood, the adhan sounds. The proud of Quraysh hear the black man's call ring out from the holiest place, and the world is turned over. So the tortured slave of Mecca becomes the first muezzin above its House.
stops.quote: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. I bear witness that there is no god but God; I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.
stops.quote_source: The Adhan (the call to prayer), as first proclaimed by Bilal
suggested_refs: The roof and door of the Kaaba
the maqam of Bilal tradition

stops.name: The valley of Hunayn — pride humbled, victory given
stops.campa: Fresh from the Opening of Mecca, twelve thousand march on the Hawazin, and some are pleased at their own numbers. In the narrow valley of Hunayn the enemy's archers ambush them from the heights and the great host breaks and flees, until only a handful stand about the Messenger. He does not move, calling them by name back to him, and God sends down His calm and armies unseen. The line re-forms, the Hawazin are routed. So the faithful learn that victory is never in their numbers but in God alone. The last of Arabia bows.
stops.quote: God has helped you on many fields, and on the day of Hunayn, when you were pleased with your great numbers, but they availed you nothing... then God sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and the believers.
suggested_refs: the valley of Hunayn (Wadi Hunayn), on the Mecca–Taif road
Quran 9 (At-Tawba) in an early manuscript

stops.name: Mount Arafat — the Farewell Pilgrimage and the Sermon
stops.campa: In the tenth year he leads the pilgrimage himself, and on the plain of Arafat, mounted on Qaswa before a great multitude, he preaches his Farewell Sermon. He declares the blood and property of every man sacred as this day; he abolishes the old feuds and usury; he charges them to be kind to women and to hold fast to the Book. Then descends the verse: This day I have perfected for you your religion. Have I conveyed the message? he asks three times, and the crowd answers Yes. O God, bear witness, he says.
stops.quote: O people, verily your blood and your property are sacred and inviolable to one another, like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours.
stops.quote_source: The Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada'), 9 Dhu al-Hijja 10 AH
suggested_refs: The Mount of Mercy (Jabal al-Rahmah) at Arafat
Masjid Namirah, Arafat
Quran 5:3 in calligraphy
sources: Farewell Sermon (Ibn Ishaq; hadith of Jabir, Sahih Muslim)

stops.name: Medina — the last illness in Aisha's chamber
stops.campa: Back in Medina a fever takes him. Too weak to lead, he bids Abu Bakr guide the prayers, and asks to be nursed in the chamber of Aisha, against whose breast he leans. He frees his slaves, gives away the last coins in the house, and warns against making his grave a place of worship. In his final hours he dips his hand in water to cool his face and murmurs of the struggle of the soul departing, and of the highest companions. He raises his finger to the One God, and is gone.
stops.quote: There is no god but God. O God, the highest companions — to the highest Companion.
stops.quote_source: Aisha's narration of the Prophet's death (Sahih al-Bukhari)
suggested_refs: The Sacred Chamber (al-Hujra al-Sharifa), Al-Masjid an-Nabawi
the Mothers of the Believers named in calligraphy
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (the death of the Prophet)

stops.name: Medina — the grave beneath the Green Dome
stops.campa: He dies on a Monday in Rabi al-Awwal, in the eleventh year of the Hijra, and grief overwhelms the city; Umar will not believe it until Abu Bakr steadies them all: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead; whoever worships God, God is living. As he counselled, they bury a prophet where he dies — in the very floor of Aisha's chamber, beside the mosque he raised. Over that spot the ages will lift the Green Dome of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, and the road that began at the Kaaba of Abraham comes to rest in the earth of Medina.
stops.quote: Whoever used to worship Muhammad, Muhammad is dead; and whoever used to worship God, God is Alive and shall never die.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr's address, in Sahih al-Bukhari; citing Quran 3:144
suggested_refs: The Green Dome (al-Qubba al-Khadra) over the grave, Al-Masjid an-Nabawi
the Rawda between the pulpit and the chamber
the Prophet's Mosque, Medina
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (the death of the Prophet)
